query: For high-entropy alloys intended as intermediate materials in plasma-facing reactor components, what single intervention could improve heat-transfer capability while preserving structural integrity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the expected outcome compared with current intermediate-layer performance, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Controlled thermal-gradient annealing to induce directional grain-boundary engineering in high-entropy alloy intermediate layers will enhance heat-transfer capability while preserving or improving structural integrity under plasma-facing reactor conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy intermediate layers produced via conventional processing methods, exhibiting an equiaxed grain structure with moderate thermal conductivity and acceptable mechanical strength.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal-gradient annealing treatment to induce directional grain alignment and form elongated, columnar grain structures.
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions (>700°C) and high cyclic mechanical loading, representative of plasma-facing reactor environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of directional grain boundaries and elongated, columnar grains that act as continuous channels for heat transport while retaining grain interlocking that supports mechanical integrity.
generation.mechanism: The thermal-gradient annealing treatment drives preferential grain growth along the imposed gradient, thereby aligning the grain boundaries into continuous pathways. These pathways facilitate more efficient heat conduction while the retained interlocking grain structures maintain or improve the mechanical strength under extreme thermal and mechanical stresses.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in measured thermal conductivity compared to the as-fabricated state, with mechanical strength maintained or improved under high temperature and cyclic load conditions.
generation.baseline: Performance of as-fabricated high-entropy alloy intermediate layers with an equiaxed microstructure.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is dependent on precisely controlled thermal gradients; if the thermal treatment is not optimized, excessive grain growth may occur, potentially compromising mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative improvement in thermal conductivity and the balance with mechanical strength under actual reactor conditions remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of high-entropy alloy intermediate layers: one set subjected to the controlled thermal-gradient annealing process and a control set processed conventionally. Expose both sets to simulated reactor conditions—temperatures above 700°C and cyclic mechanical loading.
measurements: Thermal conductivity measurements across the layers
Mechanical strength tests (tensile, compressive, cyclic load tests)
Microstructural analysis using EBSD to assess grain alignment and the formation of columnar structures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in thermal conductivity compared to the control, or if they show reduced mechanical strength under high-temperature and mechanical loading conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

decision.trend: Early work on high‐entropy alloys has largely focused on tailoring the composition and processing routes to achieve the desired structural integrity. Several studies (e.g., PMC10890668 and PMC12843301) have shown that non‐conventional solid‐state processing (such as additive friction stir deposition and plasma arc approaches) can refine the microstructure and improve mechanical performance. Research in transition layers (PMC11989606) has demonstrated that interface engineering via matching thermal expansion and bonding can mitigate cracking under thermal and mechanical stress. However, these approaches typically only managed to enhance either heat-transfer or mechanical properties – not both simultaneously.
decision.unsolved: The crucial gap remains how to boost heat-transfer capability in the intermediate HEA layers while preserving, or even enhancing, their structural integrity under the extreme thermal and mechanical loading typical of plasma-facing reactor conditions.
decision.lever: directional grain-boundary engineering via controlled thermal-gradient annealing
decision.why: Given the trend that processing routes refining microstructure (as seen in AFSD and plasma arc techniques) have improved mechanical strength, the next plausible intervention is to tailor the microstructural architecture specifically to facilitate heat transport. By using a controlled thermal or thermomechanical treatment to induce a grain alignment—where elongated, directional grains or continuous interfaces act as thermal conduits—the alloy can provide enhanced heat-transfer channels while retaining its mechanical integrity. This lever directly addresses the gap indicated by previous studies and meets the constraints of a single intervention.
